status: Actual protective-feature/function task on unchanged design claim; no new equipment or force-law topic.

helmet.publisher: US Consumer Product Safety Commission, publication 349, May 2022
helmet.readScope: Actual two-page text, especially protection, correct activity/fit and crushable-liner/replacement paragraphs read. Screenshot calls did not provide an inspectable image, so no visual layout/image claim.
helmet.facts: A suitable bicycle-helmet liner deforms to take up impact energy, reducing what reaches the head. This protection depends on appropriate activity, fit and condition; a helmet is not a guarantee against concussion or every injury.
helmet.limits: No copied figures/table, Canadian standards/legal requirement, purchase advice or new specific clinical mechanism. Do not test or modify a helmet or treat a used-impact helmet as serviceable from its appearance.

belt-mechanism.publisher: US Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration, dated 15 April 2014
belt-mechanism.facts: A restraint keeps a person within the vehicle, distributes loading over appropriate stronger body regions and allows slowing over a longer interval.
belt-mechanism.limits: An explanation of protection does not mean a belt exerts no force, prevents every injury or substitutes for correctly fitted child restraints.

belt-fit.publisher: US National Highway Traffic Safety Administration
belt-fit.readScope: Actual main overview, adult protection/fit and child-fit reference sections read; videos, linked charts and entire wider page not claimed.
belt-fit.facts: The restraint routes forces through suitable pelvis/chest regions rather than soft abdomen; correct fit matters and children may require an appropriate child restraint/booster.
belt-fit.limits: No current statistic, child-size threshold, US legal rule or pupil-specific fit determination is adopted.

helmet.feature: Appropriate crushable protective liner held correctly in place
helmet.harmfulEffect: A collision can cause rapid loading of the head.
helmet.mechanism: The supplied account explains how controlled deformation takes up some impact energy instead of transmitting it all directly to the head; the liner has a limited capacity and the correct fit keeps protection in the intended location.
helmet.limit: Not every helmet fits every activity or repeated impact; do not infer concussion prevention, invulnerability or a new clinical result.
helmet.changedCase: An original fictional look-alike shell lacks a protective liner, or the protective part shifts away from its intended position. Explain why appearance/rigidity alone does not establish the stated mechanism.

belt.feature: Correctly routed restraint connecting occupant to vehicle
belt.harmfulEffect: During rapid slowing an unrestrained person can continue moving into the vehicle interior or out of it.
belt.mechanism: The belt applies a stopping interaction while directing/distributing loading to suitable stronger body regions and increasing the slowing interval relative to an abrupt hard impact. Protection changes how the force acts; it does not erase it.
belt.limit: Use a supplied appropriate adult-sized or correctly restrained model case, not a decision about a particular child. No guarantee all injuries are prevented, no airbag-only or loose-belt substitute.
belt.changedCase: In a clearly fictional diagram description, a strap is absent or wrongly routed through a soft region. Identify the changed force pathway and missing protection facts, without an actual crash demonstration.

preparation: Provide the two original attributed feature→harmful effect→mechanism→limit case cards and blank explanation record. No learner impact tests, equipment alteration or real crash are needed.

The existing whole design claim still includes features/purpose in a familiar product, an environment and a service. Retain those varied examples separately; these two protective products do not establish whole mastery by themselves.
learnerActions: Use BOTH cases. Describe what feature is designed, which harmful force effect it changes, how that change helps and one actual limitation. A name or wear-it rule is insufficient.

Compare absorption/deformation in the liner with restraint/distribution in the belt. Explain why protective equipment can apply/transmit a force while reducing harmful effects, rather than saying it makes forces disappear.

Explain each supplied changed case and identify why a look-alike, missing part or wrong pathway does not establish the same protection. Separate an authoritative provided fact from an observation made in class.
successEvidence: Two specific feature→force effect→protection explanations with stated limits and changed-case reasoning.
Cites the actual supplied mechanism rather than style, generic safety praise or a new quantitative impulse/pressure calculation.
nearMisses: Only names helmet and seat belt or repeats a safety instruction.
Says the equipment removes every force/prevents every injury.
Treats a harder-looking shell or looser restraint as automatically safer, without its actual mechanism/fit.
protocol.transfer: Compare a fictional protective design with a missing/changed functional part; explain what the supplied facts support and why an untested design is not certified safe.
